question: In adults who had an orthopaedic implant inserted, was a record of every implant (manufacturer, size and unique identifier or lot number) placed in the patient's notes?
why: A missing implant record blocks recall, revision planning and registry returns. The corpus has one audit of the 'prosthetic pause' check [1204] but none of the implant record left in the notes.

standard.source: NatSSIPs 2 (CPOC 2023), Sequential Standard: Implant Verification, 'During the procedure'
standard.wording: A record of the implants used must be made in the patient's records. Appropriate details should be shared with the patient after the procedure. When a manufacturer's label is available, this should be placed in the notes. When it is not, for example with electronic patient records, the following should be recorded: Manufacturer; Style; Size; Manufacturer's unique identifier for the implant, or the serial number; Expiry date

pass: Every implant used (including each screw set, plate, nail, prosthetic component and cement) appears in the notes or EPR, either as a label or with manufacturer, size and unique identifier or lot number.
population: Include adults with any implant inserted in orthopaedic theatres (trauma and elective). Exclude temporary items meant for removal (K-wires removed in clinic, external fixator pins).
sample: 40 consecutive implant cases from the theatre system over the last 4 weeks (about 20 trauma, 20 elective).
data_source: Theatre management system (implant list, procedure); scanned implant label sheet or EPR implant module; operation note.

question: In adults aged 65 or over, or with an eGFR below 60, listed for elective hip or knee replacement, did the pre-operative assessment record their risk of acute kidney injury?
why: Post-operative AKI after arthroplasty is common and often linked to NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors. The single orthopaedic AKI audit in the corpus looks at care after AKI [1180], not risk assessment before surgery.

standard.wording: Assess the risk of acute kidney injury in adults before surgery. Be aware that increased risk is associated with: emergency surgery, especially when the person has sepsis or hypovolaemia; intraperitoneal surgery; chronic kidney disease (adults with an eGFR less than 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 are at particular risk); diabetes; heart failure; age 65 years or over; liver disease; use of drugs that can cause or exacerbate kidney injury in the perioperative period (in particular, NSAIDs after surgery). Use the risk assessment to inform a clinical management plan.

pass: Pre-op record documents AKI risk and a plan for ACE inhibitors/ARBs, diuretics and post-op NSAIDs (hold, continue or avoid).
population: Include adults aged 65+ or with eGFR <60 listed for elective primary hip or knee replacement. Exclude patients on renal replacement therapy.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: Pre-op assessment record; lab system (eGFR); medication list; post-op drug chart (NSAID prescribed); post-op creatinine.

Pass criterion

close_loop: Present to pre-op assessment nurses and arthroplasty team. If it worked, keep the template box and track post-op AKI rate.

question: In orthopaedic ward patients with suspected infection and a NEWS2 score of 7 or more, were IV antibiotics given within 1 hour of that score?
why: Post-operative sepsis on orthopaedic wards is less common than in medicine and teams are less practised. The corpus has ward sepsis audits in medicine [2618] but none on orthopaedic wards.

standard.wording: Give people aged 16 or over who are at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic treatment, within 1 hour of calculating the person's NEWS2 score on initial assessment in the emergency department or on ward deterioration.

pass: First IV antibiotic dose administered within 60 minutes of the first NEWS2 ≥7 recorded with suspected infection.
population: Include adult orthopaedic inpatients with a NEWS2 of 7 or more and suspected or confirmed infection. Exclude patients on an end-of-life pathway and those already on IV antibiotics for that episode.
sample: All eligible episodes over the last 6–12 months (expect 30–40), found from e-observations NEWS2 ≥7 reports.
data_source: E-observations (NEWS2 time); medical notes (suspected infection, review time); e-prescribing administration record (antibiotic time); lab system (lactate, cultures).

change: Set e-observations so a NEWS2 ≥7 on an orthopaedic ward pages the on-call doctor with a sepsis screen, and stock a sepsis grab bag with first-dose antibiotics on each orthopaedic ward.
reaudit: Week 13–14 onwards: all eligible episodes in the following 3 months, same template.
close_loop: Present with the sepsis/deteriorating patient team. If it worked, keep the paging rule and grab bags and add orthopaedic wards to the trust sepsis dashboard.
evidence: [2618] ward sepsis protocol audit: proforma used 13.9%, sepsis 6 bundle 55.5% (no re-audit)

question: In adults discharged with opioids after orthopaedic surgery, did the discharge letter state the opioid dose, amount supplied and planned duration?
why: Unclear discharge opioid plans lead to repeat prescriptions and long-term use. Orthopaedic opioid audits in the corpus look at inpatient prescribing [1298], not the discharge letter.

standard.source: Faculty of Pain Medicine / RCoA 'Surgery and Opioids: Best Practice Guidelines 2021', Discharge Planning 3 and 4
standard.wording: The hospital discharge letter should be available in a timely way and provided to all healthcare professionals involved in caring for the patient, including community pharmacists, to avoid an acute prescription of opioids inadvertently becoming a repeat prescription. The hospital discharge letter must explicitly state the recommended opioid dose, amount supplied and planned duration of use. ... Usually 5 days and no more than 7 days of opioids (including Tramadol) should be prescribed.

pass: Discharge letter states opioid dose, amount supplied and planned duration or stop date, and supply is 7 days or less.
population: Include adults discharged on any opioid (including tramadol and codeine) after orthopaedic surgery. Exclude patients on opioids for over 3 months before admission (opioid tolerant) and palliative care.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible discharges over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Electronic discharge summary / TTO; pharmacy dispensing record (quantity supplied).

Pass criterion: all three items stated and ≤7 days

change: Add a required 'opioid plan' block (dose, quantity, stop date, GP not to add to repeats) to the discharge TTO template when any opioid is prescribed.
close_loop: Present with the acute pain team and pharmacy. If it worked, keep the TTO block and share it with the local GP prescribing group.
evidence: [1298] primary THR: NG180 posters and teaching increased regular D0 oral opioid prescribing by 30% (inpatient step only)
[1207] hip fracture discharge letter proforma: compliance to 95% (template works)
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from discharge letters

question: In orthopaedic inpatients with Parkinson's disease, was every dose of their Parkinson's medicine given within 30 minutes of the prescribed time in the first 72 hours?
why: Missed or late doses around surgery and fasting cause rigidity, falls and aspiration. Existing audits are in elderly care [1890] [1165]; the orthopaedic audit of pre-op medicines [1630] did not isolate Parkinson's drugs.

standard.wording: 1.3.2 Antiparkinsonian medicines should not be withdrawn abruptly or allowed to fail suddenly due to poor absorption (for example, gastroenteritis, abdominal surgery) to avoid the potential for acute akinesia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome. 1.3.4 In view of the risks of sudden changes in antiparkinsonian medicines, people with Parkinson's disease who are admitted to hospital or care homes should have their medicines: given at the appropriate times, which in some cases may mean allowing self-medication; adjusted by, or adjusted only after discussion with, a specialist in the management of Parkinson's disease.

pass: All Parkinson's medicine doses due in the first 72 hours given within 30 minutes of the prescribed time (local definition of 'appropriate times'), including during nil-by-mouth periods.
population: Include adult orthopaedic inpatients with Parkinson's disease on levodopa or dopamine agonists. Exclude patients on end-of-life care.
sample: All eligible admissions over the last 12 months (expect 30–40), from pharmacy or e-prescribing search for Parkinson's drugs on orthopaedic wards.
data_source: E-prescribing administration record (prescribed and given times); ED record; anaesthetic chart; notes (NBM plan).

target: ≥90% of patients with all doses on time

close_loop: Present with pharmacy and the Parkinson's nurse specialist. If it worked, keep the alerts and include orthopaedic wards in the trust time-critical medicines audit.

effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from e-prescribing

question: In adults having elective primary hip or knee replacement, was a urinary catheter avoided unless a clinical indication was documented?
why: Routine catheters add waste, infection and delay mobilisation. The Green Theatre Checklist lists catheterisation as an avoidable intervention. Orthopaedic catheter audits in the corpus are in hip fracture [1208], not elective arthroplasty.

standard.source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 8
standard.wording: Avoid clinically unnecessary interventions (e.g. antibiotics, urinary catheterisation, histology examinations)

pass: No urinary catheter inserted in theatre, or a catheter with a documented indication (e.g. retention history, long case, critical fluid balance).
population: Include adults having elective primary total hip or knee replacement. Exclude simultaneous bilateral and revision cases.
sample: 40 consecutive elective primary hip or knee replacements over the last 6 weeks.
data_source: Anaesthetic chart and theatre nursing record (catheter inserted and reason); ward notes (removal time, retention, CAUTI).

Pass criterion

change: Remove catheter packs from the default arthroplasty pick list and add 'catheter: indication' to the Team Brief.
close_loop: Present at theatre users' group and the trust green team. If it worked, keep the pick list change and report catheters and waste avoided.
evidence: [1869] ED older adults: catheter indication documented 36% (guideline created; no re-audit)
[1738] WaSTE multicentre arthroplasty audit: ~14 kg waste per case, mostly infectious stream (no re-audit)
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from anaesthetic and nursing records

question: In adults having hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement for hip fracture, was the femoral head sent for histology only when a clinical indication was documented?
why: Routine femoral head histology uses lab time, formalin and transport for little yield. The Green Theatre Checklist names histology as an avoidable intervention. No audit in the corpus.

sample: 40 consecutive cases over the last 2–3 months.
